title: Blackstone's Next $50 Billion in India Will Go Beyond Offices and Malls
excerpt: The firm plans to double India exposure to $100 billion in five years, expanding from real estate into infrastructure, credit, healthcare and data centres.
body:
• Blackstone has about $50 billion invested in India and plans to double that to $100 billion over the next five years, president and COO Jonathan Gray said in interviews this month.
  • The next $50 billion is set to spread beyond the offices, malls and warehouses that built the firm's India name, into infrastructure, private credit and growth investing.
  • Gray named healthcare, financial services, travel and digital infrastructure — data centres, neoclouds and renewables — as the high-growth areas the firm is targeting.
  • Currency depreciation is the biggest headwind for foreign investors in India, Gray said, which is why the firm favours fast-growing businesses over flat, bond-like returns.

Blackstone plans to double its India investments to $100 billion over the next five years, from about $50 billion today, and the new money will not simply buy more of what made the firm India's best-known foreign landlord. In interviews with The Economic Times and CNBC-TV18, president and chief operating officer Jonathan Gray said the expansion will run mainly through private equity and real estate, and widen into infrastructure, credit and growth investing, according to Mint's account of the interviews.

Beyond offices and malls

Real estate built Blackstone's India position: about $22 billion of property, more than 150 million square feet of office and retail space, and five of the country's six listed real estate investment trusts, including a $1.3 billion secondary sale in Knowledge Realty Trust in August. Gray said that portfolio — logistics, hotels and shopping centres included — is performing well. But the growth list he laid out is broader: healthcare, financial services, travel, manufacturing and the physical backbone of artificial intelligence. AI opportunities span data centres, neoclouds and IT services, he told The Times of India, with renewables needed to power the build-out. Most data centres, he noted, are backed by 15- to 20-year contracts with investment-grade hyperscalers, which limits speculative construction.

"In a developed market, you might be buying existing businesses or real estate. Here, you have to be a builder."

— Jonathan Gray, President and COO, Blackstone

The operating footprint is growing too

The investment target is arriving alongside an operational one. Blackstone has opened a global capability centre in Bengaluru — its first outside the United States — to support finance, technology, legal, compliance and human resources work for its global teams, according to StartupTalky. The centre, led by senior managing director Susan Yung, has about 80 staff and expects to pass 100 by the end of the year; Mumbai, the firm's India headquarters, has about 90, taking the India headcount to roughly 170. Vice-chairman and CFO Michael Chae said the Bengaluru team will be integrated with global operations rather than run as a standalone back office. The firm's global assets under management have quadrupled in a decade to about $1.4 trillion.

What could slow it down

Gray was direct about the frictions. Currency depreciation has been the biggest headwind for foreign investors, he said, eroding dollar returns and making high-growth businesses a better bet than assets with flat returns. He also repeated Blackstone's call to ease India's delisting rules: the 90 percent shareholding threshold required to take a company private is among the highest in the world. On AI, he acknowledged a risk of overinvestment but pointed to portfolio evidence of returns — at IGI, the firm's diamond certification business in India, AI visualisation tools grade stones 40 percent faster and let each employee process 30 percent more diamonds.

Why Blackstone is still bullish

The case rests on growth and on exits. Gray cited India's expanding middle class, infrastructure build-out and technology workforce, and put GDP per capita at about $3,000 — roughly one-thirtieth of the US level — as a measure of the headroom. He also praised India's capital markets: Blackstone has completed 14 IPOs in India, and Gray called the market an underappreciated asset for foreign investors. "As long as the economy continues to grow, and the government continues to support that growth with policies that give foreign investors certainty and clarity, I think the opportunity set will grow," he said. For Indian founders and fund managers, the practical read is that the world's largest alternative asset manager is hiring, building and looking for platforms in healthcare, financial services and digital infrastructure — sectors where cheques of this size usually go to businesses that can absorb them at scale.
